analysis.one_liner: Requires money transfer companies to disclose exchange rates and fees on international remittances.
analysis.headline: The bill won 71 cosponsors from both parties but died in a House committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require any bank or money transfer business sending money abroad for a customer to tell that customer, before the transaction: the exchange rate it is using, the market exchange rate for comparison, all fees charged, and the exact amount the recipient will get abroad. The same information would have to appear on receipts, in advertisements, and in the language the business mainly uses to talk to its customers.
analysis.who_benefits: People who send money to family members in other countries, largely immigrants and their families, who today often cannot see how much a transfer company takes from them through a padded exchange rate or hidden fees before anything is disclosed. The bill forces the full cost out into the open before they commit to the transaction.

how_it_helps.text: Requires businesses to disclose the exchange rate they use and the market exchange rate in the destination country, so customers can see the markup for the first time.
Requires disclosure of all commissions and fees, and the exact amount of foreign currency the recipient will receive, before the transaction is completed and printed on the receipt.
Requires the same information in print, broadcast, and electronic advertising, and in the language the business mainly uses at that location if not English.

analysis.who_pays: Money transfer companies and banks, whose profit on international transfers partly comes from exchange-rate markups and fees that would now have to be disclosed on the storefront, on receipts, and in every advertisement. Some compliance cost for printing and posting disclosures falls on small remittance and check-cashing businesses as well.

drawbacks.text: The bill adds disclosure paperwork and signage requirements that fall hardest on small check-cashing and currency-exchange businesses, and some of that cost could be passed on to customers.

Disclosure alone does not cap prices: a customer can see a large exchange-rate markup and still have no alternative provider in their neighborhood, so the bill may not lower costs where remittance agents face no competition.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and cheap: making the true cost of a transfer visible before the customer pays is a low-cost, well-established kind of consumer protection, and the main honest objection is that disclosure alone does not create competition where none exists.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee and then to its consumer credit subcommittee, where it stayed until the Congress ended without a hearing, a vote, or movement toward one.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 29, 2001, by Rep. Luis Gutierrez with 71 cosponsors, including 3 Republicans and the chamber's lone Independent.
It was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services on the day it was introduced.
On April 10, 2001, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit, and no further action was recorded for the rest of the Congress.
The bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote, and it expired when the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Money transfer companies and banks keep charging whatever exchange-rate markups and fees the market allows, with no requirement to show customers the comparison rate. Consumers sending remittances remain unable to see the true cost before paying.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was heavily Democratic but not exclusively: 67 of 208 House Democrats, 3 of 223 House Republicans, and the chamber's sole Independent cosponsored, and no party ever voted on the bill.

industries.note: These businesses would have to post their exchange rate, the market comparison rate, and every fee on the storefront, receipts, and advertising, making their exchange-rate markup visible for the first time. Their interest in the bill ran against the customers sending remittances, since the markup is part of their revenue.

industries.industry: Check cashing and currency exchange businesses
industries.note: Included in the bill's definition of money transmitting businesses, they would face new signage, receipt, and advertising disclosure requirements in multiple languages, and their remittance pricing would become comparable at a glance.

The bill's disclosure requirements apply to financial institutions initiating international transfers whether or not the customer holds an account, exposing fees and exchange-rate spreads on wire services.
